answer:
I ran one job on IQM's free Garnet test device, garnet:mock. The job ID is 01a1609d-09ad-705e-b973-affa5d3539b4. It held 6 circuits, one for each moment in time: t = 0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.2, 1.6 and 2.0. Each circuit ran 2000 shots. The test device costs no credits.

What I built. Each of the 6 qubits stands for one copper spin. Every circuit starts with the spins set to up, down, up, down, up, down. It then lets the spins interact under the Heisenberg model with J = 1. A quantum computer cannot apply the whole interaction in one go, so the circuit applies it in small time steps of 0.2 or less. That means 2 steps for t = 0.4 and 10 steps for t = 2.0. I checked the step error against an exact calculation. The two differ by less than 0.01 at every moment. The server received circuits with 0, 28, 58, 88, 118 and 148 two-qubit (CZ) gates.

What a perfect quantum computer would show. I simulated the exact circuits the server received, with no noise. Neel order is 1 for the perfect up-down pattern. It reads 1.00 at t = 0, 0.88 at t = 0.4, 0.62 at t = 0.8, 0.41 at t = 1.2, 0.35 at t = 1.6 and 0.38 at t = 2.0. The order falls fast at first. It then levels off and wobbles near 0.35 to 0.4. The exact physics gives almost the same numbers: 1.00, 0.88, 0.62, 0.41, 0.34 and 0.37.

What the test device gave back. The measured Neel order was -0.21, -0.39, -0.42, -0.39, -0.42 and -0.39. These numbers carry no physics. The mock device does not run the circuit. It returns 4 placeholder bit patterns, each about 500 times, for every circuit. One example is 000000, 111111, 011011 and 100100. Even the t = 0 circuit, which should give 1.00 every time, came back at -0.21. So the test device confirms that the job was accepted, compiled and ran end to end. It tells us nothing about the physics. A real device such as Garnet or Emerald would be needed for real numbers. Expect noise there. The circuit for t = 2 has 148 CZ gates, and that much noise would pull the result toward 0.

The principle. In the up-down pattern, each spin points opposite to its neighbors. That pattern is not a resting state of the Heisenberg model. The Sx Sx and Sy Sy terms swap a neighboring up and down pair. Each swap spreads the pattern into a quantum mix of many arrangements. These are quantum fluctuations. They act even with no heat at all, and they wear the perfect order down from 1 to about 0.4 within a time of about 1/J.

What this says about KCuF3. In the real crystal the copper spins form long chains that are almost one-dimensional. Quantum fluctuations are strong in such chains. Theory and neutron scattering experiments agree that a perfect one-dimensional Heisenberg chain never settles into a fixed up-down pattern, even at absolute zero. KCuF3 only orders below about 39 K, and it orders only because of weak couplings between the chains. Even then, each copper spin keeps a much smaller ordered moment than a classical magnet would give. Its excitations are spinons, which are half-spin pieces, and not ordinary spin waves. This 6-spin run shows the same effect on a small scale: the textbook up-down picture melts quickly. Two caveats apply. Six spins is a very short chain, so the level near 0.4 and the wobble are partly finite-size effects. The facts above about the real material come from known physics and were not measured here.
